To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the class gradient is not as large as it appears; (2) the gradient is explained away by the effects of employment status and unobservable heterogeneity; (3) employment status is a causal pathway by which the gradient transpires; (4) employment status has an independent gradient in its own right; and (5) the gradient in employment status has not widened over time.

(1) there is a class gradient in psychological wellbeing; (2) this gradient cannot be explained away with unobserved individual heterogeneity; (3) the effects of social class are largely explained by employment status; (4) there is a gradient between employment and unemployment; (5) the effects of class and employment on psychological wellbeing do not change significantly over time.

employment status is the most important pathway by which social class inequalities in psychological well-being are transmitted and that the social class gradient in mental ill-health has been stable over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between social class and mental health and the role of employment status in that relationship.
the social patterning of mental health and its changes over time.
the relationship between social class and psychological well being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a social class gradient, but it is small and not worsening over time.
social class is associated with psychological well-being but the association is not large and is not worsening over time.
social class is not a significant source of inequality in mental health, though the evidence for this is not conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the class gradient in psychological health is substantial, and that it has changed very little over time.
class inequalities in psychological well-being have not worsened over time.
the social class gradient in mental wellbeing is substantial and that employment status is an important confounder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the class gradient is not a simple story.
the class gradient in mental well-being is not a simple matter of class disadvantage.
employment status is an important factor in understanding the class gradient in mental well-being.
